candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.8833 malware probability, but the supplied evidence does not show cryptojacking-specific behavior. All 18 positive-SHAP n-grams are generic x86 compiler idioms: function prologue/epilogue and stack handling (MOV LEAVE, LEAVE RET, MOV PUSH, CALL PUSH, ADD POP, LEA POP), call setup and cleanup (CALL ADD, CALL CMP, LEA CALL, XOR CALL), and basic conditional logic (TEST JS, MOV JZ, CMP CMOVZ, CMOVZ MOV). None of them are the arithmetic, rotate or shift, or tight-loop patterns normally linked to hashing or mining kernels. Of the top 20 n-grams, 13 have a relative frequency of 0.000000, so their positive SHAP values come from absence, not from observed code. Only ADD ADD is notably frequent (0.392982, SHAP +0.013618). That frequency is unusually high, and it could mean data or padding decoded as code, or unusual code structure. The evidence does not say which, so it cannot be tied to mining. MOV TEST (0.021053, SHAP -0.006484) pushes toward benign. No function names or locations were provided for any n-gram, so nothing can be attributed to a specific routine. The model's score is high, but the evidence is statistical and non-specific, so the result is suspicious yet inconclusive.

candidate_analysis.recommended_action: Do not treat this as confirmed cryptojacking from this evidence alone. Check the ADD ADD concentration to see whether it comes from real code, padding, or data decoded as instructions, and look for packing.
